title: What Happens If You Disagree With Your Architect? Here's How We Handle It
excerpt: Design disagreements happen on renovation projects. Here's what to expect when you and your architect see things differently, and how a design-build firm in Westchester handles it.
content:
You're excited about your kitchen remodel or home addition. You've hired an architect. Then the first set of drawings comes back and something feels off. Maybe the layout doesn't work for how you actually live. Maybe the style doesn't match your vision. Maybe the budget implications make you nervous. What happens now?

Disagreements between homeowners and architects are normal. They happen on projects in Scarsdale, Pelham, Rye, and everywhere else in Westchester County. The question isn't whether you'll disagree. It's how the architect responds when you do.

Why Disagreements Happen in the First Place

Most conflicts come from a gap between what you imagined and what ended up on paper. You might have explained your vision clearly, or you might have been vague. The architect might have listened well, or might have made assumptions. Both things are usually true to some degree.

Sometimes the disagreement is about practical concerns. A licensed architect in Westchester, NY might propose a design that's beautiful but doesn't work with your town's building codes or your home's existing structure. Other times it's personal taste. You want modern. They sketched transitional. Neither is wrong, but they're not aligned.

In towns like Mamaroneck, Harrison, and White Plains, you're also dealing with local building departments that have their own requirements. A design might need adjusting just to get permit approval. When homeowners aren't prepared for that, it can feel like the architect is fighting against them.

What a Design-Build Approach Does Differently

When your architect is also a general contractor, disagreements get resolved faster. There's no separate company to blame. There's one person responsible for the whole project.

At House Architecture & Construction, Silvio M. Luca is both a licensed architect and general contractor in Westchester. He runs every project personally. That means when you have concerns about a design, he's not handing you off to the construction team to figure out later. He's thinking about buildability, code compliance, and cost from the start.

If you're planning a second-story addition in Bronxville or a primary suite addition in Larchmont, a design-build approach means the person drawing it up has already built dozens of similar projects. They know what works and what creates headaches during construction. That knowledge gets built into the design before you ever see the drawings.

How to Handle It When You Disagree

First, speak up early. Don't sit on concerns hoping they'll resolve themselves. A good architect wants feedback. If something doesn't feel right, say so immediately.

Second, be specific about what bothers you. "I don't like it" is harder to work with than "The kitchen feels too small for entertaining" or "I'm worried this won't fit our budget." Specific feedback points to a real problem that can be solved.

Third, understand that sometimes the architect is protecting you from a mistake. When you're doing home renovations in Westchester County, permit requirements matter. The design might need to stay within certain lines. That's not the architect being stubborn. That's the architect keeping your project on track.

At House Architecture & Construction, disagreements get addressed through conversation, not paperwork. If you're unhappy with a design direction, Silvio works with you to understand what's actually bothering you and finds a path forward. That might mean revising the drawings. It might mean explaining why a different approach will work better. It's honest dialogue.

The Real Advantage of Having One Person in Charge

When you hire a residential architect in Scarsdale or anywhere else in Westchester, you're often getting a designer who then hands off the project to a contractor they've never worked with before. Those two people might have different priorities. The architect cares about the design. The contractor cares about the build. Sometimes that creates problems during construction that could have been prevented.

A design-build firm in Westchester eliminates that split. The person designing your custom home in Westchester County is the same person building it. When you disagree about something, it gets resolved by someone who understands both sides of the problem.

If you're considering home additions in Westchester or any other type of project, disagreements with your architect don't have to derail the work. They usually just mean clarification is needed.
